title: Aggregate Functions
summary: An aggregate function turns several rows into one answer, such as a count, total or average.
introduction: An aggregate function turns several rows into one answer, such as a count, total or average. Count the books in a table or add their prices. Read how missing values affect the answer before choosing a function.
learningObjectives: Count rows and distinct values with COUNT
Compute totals, averages and extremes with SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
Avoid integer division and non-portable bare columns

blocks.text: From many rows to one value

An aggregate function takes a column (or expression) across all the rows that survive the WHERE clause and returns one value. Without GROUP BY (next lesson) the whole table is a single group, so the result has exactly one row.

blocks.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(quantity) AS items FROM orders;

rows: Number of rows where col is not NULL
Smallest and largest value (numbers, text or dates)

blocks.code:
SELECT MIN(price) AS cheapest,
       MAX(price) AS priciest,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average
FROM products;

blocks.text: `AVG` returns a floating-point number with many decimals (26.123333...), so wrapping it in `ROUND(..., 2)` keeps the output tidy.

All aggregates except `COUNT(*)` skip NULL values. That is usually what you want (an average over unknown values would be meaningless), but it means `COUNT(column)` can be smaller than `COUNT(*)`, and `AVG` of a column with NULLs divides by the number of known values only.

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE TABLE tickets (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, assignee TEXT
OK: INSERT INTO tickets (title, assignee) VALUES

all_rows | assigned | people
---------+----------+-------
3        | 1        | 1

blocks.text: WHERE filters the rows *before* they are aggregated, so counting US customers is just an aggregate over a filtered table:

blocks.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS us_customers FROM customers WHERE country = 'US';

blocks.text: Aggregates work on joined rows too. Total revenue multiplies each order's quantity by the product's price and sums the results:

Dividing two integers gives an integer in SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server: `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`. MySQL and Oracle are the exceptions and return 3.5. Make one operand a decimal (`7 / 2.0`) or cast it (`CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2`) when you need the fraction. `AVG` is safe: it always returns a floating-point result.

blocks.code:
SELECT 7 / 2 AS integer_division,
       7 / 2.0 AS real_division,
       AVG(quantity) AS avg_quantity
FROM orders;

blocks.title: Mixing a plain column with an aggregate
blocks.text: `SELECT name, MAX(price) FROM products` is accepted by SQLite, which helpfully returns the name of the most expensive product, and by MySQL in some configurations, but PostgreSQL and SQL Server reject it: a column that is neither aggregated nor grouped has no defined value. Do not rely on the SQLite shortcut; use `ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 1` or a subquery, which work everywhere.

blocks.title: Works in SQLite only
blocks.code: SELECT name, MAX(price) AS top_price FROM products;

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Compute the number of orders, the largest quantity and the earliest `ordered_on` in one query, then restrict it to orders placed in February 2025 or later.

blocks.title: Try it yourself
blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders,
       MAX(quantity) AS largest,
       MIN(ordered_on) AS first_order
FROM orders;

questions.question: A column holds the values 10, NULL and 20. What does `AVG(col)` return?
questions.explanation: AVG skips NULL, so it averages 10 and 20 over two values: 15. Treating NULL as zero would give 10, which is why COALESCE(col, 0) is needed when that is what you want.

questions.question: `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(assignee)` always return the same number.
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row, COUNT(assignee) only rows where assignee is not NULL. They differ as soon as the column has NULLs.
